did_you_know.text: Did you know? Isaiah describes legislation that is not merely a moral mistake, but laws deliberately written to create injustice: “decrees of iniquity” and “laws that produce oppression.”
Did you know? Those harmed by this injustice include the poor, the needy, widows, and orphans—groups society is especially responsible for protecting.

Did you know? Assyria is called “the rod of My anger” and “the staff in their hands is My wrath”; in other words, it is presented as an instrument through which the Lord brings judgment, not as a completely independent power.
Did you know? Assyria does not understand its role as merely an instrument of judgment: its heart plans to destroy and annihilate many nations, going beyond the mission assigned to it.
Did you know? Isaiah uses the images of an ax and a saw to illustrate Assyria’s pride: just as a tool cannot boast over the person using it, Assyria cannot claim all the power and success for itself.
Did you know? The desired future of Israel’s remnant is described as a change in the source of its security: it will no longer rely on the one who struck it, but will truly rely on the Lord.
Did you know? The chapter encourages the people of Zion not to fear Assyria and promises that its yoke and oppression will be removed from Israel after the Lord’s anger has passed.

Did you know? In its final section, the chapter describes Assyria’s advance by naming many settlements, including Aiath, Migron, Michmash, Geba, Ramah, Anathoth, and Nob; this creates a sense of rapid progress toward Jerusalem.
Did you know? Although the Assyrian army reaches Nob and shakes its fist at Mount Zion, this description immediately leads to a vision in which the Lord humbles the threatening power.

Did you know? The conclusion uses the image of a forest: the thickets will be cut down with iron, and Lebanon will fall before the Mighty One. This image expresses the collapse of human pride and power.
